title: Thinking aloud in technical interviews
examples: Should I talk through my thinking even if I know the answer?
How much detail should I give when I am clarifying the problem?
Is it better to code the whole solution or just parts of it?

explain.say: When you start, you must first clarify the problem completely. Say you need to know all the rules.
Next, you must plan your approach before writing any code. Say you want to outline the steps logically.
Then, you must code the solution step by step while explaining your logic. Say you write the actual working code now.
After coding, you must test your solution with examples. Say you check it against known inputs.
In a real job interview, you must think aloud throughout the entire process. Say this shows the interviewer your thought process.
A common mistake is jumping straight to coding without planning. Say this makes your code messy and hard to follow.

faq.q: Should I stop talking if I get stuck on a problem?
faq.a: No, you should keep talking even if you are stuck. Describe what you are thinking about next.
asks: What if I don't know the answer?
Is it okay to say I am stuck?

faq.q: When should I stop clarifying the problem?
faq.a: You should stop clarifying when you feel you have covered all the constraints and edge cases.
asks: Do I need to ask questions all the time?

faq.q: Is it better to write pseudocode or actual code first?
faq.a: It is often best to write pseudocode first to solidify the logic, then translate it to code.
asks: Pseudocode vs code, what is better?
Should I write steps or syntax first?

faq.q: How do I handle a test case that fails during testing?
faq.a: When a test fails, explain why it failed. Then, adjust your plan and re-test the specific part.

faq.q: Should I worry about the time limit while I am thinking aloud?
faq.a: Focus on clarity over speed initially. A clear, slow answer is better than a fast, confusing one.
asks: Is speed more important than clarity?
How to manage time in the interview?

facts: Clarifying ensures you understand all problem boundaries.
Planning organizes your thoughts before writing code.
Testing validates that your solution works correctly.
Thinking aloud demonstrates your problem-solving process.

quiz.say: What is the primary goal of the 'clarify' stage?
quiz.show: To identify all rules and limits.

options.show: To identify all rules and limits.
options.say: To identify all rules and limits.

options.show: To write the first lines of code.
options.say: To write the first lines of code.

quiz.why: Clarifying ensures you understand all problem boundaries.

wrong.0: Testing requires a complete, coded solution first.
wrong.2: This skips the necessary planning phase.
wrong.3: Guessing is not based on facts given in the problem.

quiz.say: If your initial plan seems too complex, what should you do next?

options.show: Skip planning and move straight to coding.
options.say: Skip planning and move straight to coding.

options.show: Ignore the complexity and just code it.
options.say: Ignore the complexity and just code it.

options.show: Ask the interviewer to change the problem.
options.say: Ask the interviewer to change the problem.

quiz.why: Re-evaluating the plan helps you find the most efficient path.

wrong.0: This is the most common mistake in this process.
wrong.2: Coding without a solid plan leads to bugs.
wrong.3: This avoids solving the problem entirely.

quiz.say: When testing, if your code fails on a large input, what should you explain?

options.show: And just write the correct answer.
options.say: And just write the correct answer.

options.show: That the input was too big.
options.say: That the input was too big.

options.show: That the whole solution is wrong.
options.say: That the whole solution is wrong.

quiz.why: Pinpointing the failure shows deep understanding of the code.

wrong.0: You must explain the process of correction.
wrong.2: This blames the test case, not the code.
wrong.3: Be specific; try to isolate the error.
